newsitem.title: UK: Fuel cell elbows past battery for clean fuel lead.
newsitem.headline: Fuel cell elbows past battery for clean fuel lead.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Fuel cells and hybrid engines have overtaken the battery as the most likely powerplant for zero emission cars of the future, the Economist Intelligence Unit said in a report published Tuesday.
Improvements to the petrol engine's fuel economy are likely to marginalise diesel power too, the report said.

But despite improvements in technology, conventional petrol engines will provide 90 percent of power for the next 15 years, while fossil fuel will supply around 80 percent of the world's energy needs for at least the next 50 years, the report said.
"There will not be a major switch to battery-powered electric cars within the foreseeable future," said Jeffrey Daniels, author of the report.
"Battery-powered cars will always be too expensive and too limited in their performance. Research into advanced batteries is already being scaled back," Daniels said.
This despite recent introductions of battery powered vehicles by General Motors Corp in the U.S., and Toyota Motor Corp and Honda Motor Co of Japan.

GM has already launched its EV-1 battery powered car, but so far only plans to build a small number. Because of its high cost and maximum range of about 90 miles, GM is only leasing vehicles. It is not clear what will happen when demand from rich trend-setters has been sated.
Battery technology has been around for almost as long as the internal combustion engine, but has never made the leap from slow, limited range utility vehicle into the car.

Politicians in California tried to force car companies to produce battery-powered vehicles, but last year finally conceded that an affordable battery power car with acceptable range just wasn't going to happen.
The E.I.U. said the technology of fuel cells is now accelerating.
"The new fuel-cell device which turns a liquid fuel into electricity without the need for combustion-is one reason why research teams have scaled down battery work," Daniels said.

"There is a real possibility that vehicles with this power source will appear by 2010-2015. Mercedes-Benz has a fuel-cell powered vehicle based on its multi-purpose vehicle. Later in 1996 Toyota demonstrated a RAV-4 equipped not only with a fuel cell but also with a hybrid drivetrain," Daniels said.
"Hybrid" vehicles have two engines, a battery for use in towns, and a second more conventional engine which takes over for out-of-town driving, and also charges the battery.

Much development work for fuel cells has been done for Mercedes and Volkswagen AG by Ballard Power Systems of Vancouver, Canada. Buses powered by Ballards fuel cells will be on the street's of Chicago by 1998.

Ballard expects fuel cell powered cars to be on the road from 2003 to 2005. Ballard is banking on clean-air laws in California, Massachusetts and New York early next century to kick-start demand for these vehicles.
Other main points form the E.I.U. report include -
* Petrol engines cannot be made much cleaner, but will be 20 to 30 percent more economical, led by Mitsubishi Motors's direct-injection petrol engine.
* More economical petrol engines will relegate diesel engines to small niches like low-power small cars, and high-economy direct-injection diesels.
* Reformulated petrol, now big in the U.S. because of its low emissions, will emerge in Europe.
* Compressed natural gas engines for commercial vehicles, will lead to the development of liquefied natural gas power.
